newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Rates seen key for Indonesian economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rates seen key for Indonesian economy.

text.p: Indonesia's interest rate policy will be the key for the direction of country's economy after the float of the rupiah currency, economists said.
High short-term interest rates, imposed to quash speculation on the rupiah, could have a detrimental effect on the economy but are not expected to last long, the economists told Reuters.
Bank Indonesia ended the system of managing the exchange rate via an intervention band on Thursday to safeguard the country's reserves, effectively floating the rupiah.
The move knocked the rupiah to a historic low of 2,960 to the dollar before it recovered to close at 2,900 in Jakarta on Friday.

The rupiah has weakened by more than 20 percent so far this year with much of the losses recorded in the last few months, when economic woes in Thailand sparked a wave of speculative attacks on currencies throughout the region.
Both Thailand and the Philippines have been forced into de facto devaulations of their currencies.

The currency slump also hit Indonesia's stock market, which closed 3.94 percent lower at 617.71 points on Friday, its lowest level for the year, and discouraged bond investors from once blue-chip paper.
Bond traders said investors were only interested in Indonesian paper at a discount and even demanded a yield of at least 18 percent, forcing overall prices to fall.
The government raised short-term interest rates to support its tight monetary and fiscal policies imposed to contain the externally-induced outflow of capital.
An extended high short-term interest rate policy, combined with a sliding currency, could slow down the economy in the long-run, economists and treasurers said.
But they were confident the expensive rupiah policy would be reversed in the short-term to ease the burden on the real estate sector, which was already hit by rising dollar costs.
"The fact that the central bank was willing to let the rupiah float (indicates it will) allow interest rates to come down," said Vi fixed income strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"It means the bank believes that transmission from interest rates to the economy is much stronger than transmission from the exchange rate to the economy," Low said.
Pardy Kendy, chief treasurer at PT Bank Buana Indonesia, agreed, saying high short-term interest rates would hit every sector of the country's economy.
"I think Indonesians have experience of how to adjust to lower rupiah rates. It's nothing new for us. But my worry is the burden of high interest rates on the economy," Kendy said.
The rupiah has been devalued four times, the last in September 1986 when its lost 45 percent of its value against the U.S. currency.
It has since been pegged within the central bank's intervention band.
"I think the costs of higher dollars could still be borne, but high interest expenses will last stronger," Kendy said.
Mirza Adityaswara, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said tight monetary policy adopted briefly in 1991 had produced a series of non-performing loans in the following years.
He said that allowing the rupiah float would mean some short-term pain, but the effects would be temporary.
"Exchange rate adjustment is one-off," Adityaswara said.
Low said the problem was not unique to Indonesia.
"The problem is outside -- Asia and the general bearishness. Indonesia cannot escape it," Low said. "It's not very fundamentals-related."

Low added that economic growth would not be materially affected if interest rates could settle down to a normal level, shifting the future burden of adjustment to the exchange rate rather than to interest rates.
